Chapter six. What actually protected you.

So what really worked for European investors through the last two crashes? Three things. And none of them is a clever ETF.

Number one. Matching your money to your time horizon.

Your world ETF needed thirteen years to recover from the dot-com top. Money you need in the next five years has no business being one hundred percent in stocks.

Picture someone who's fifty-eight in 2026 and plans to retire at sixty-five. If a dot-com style crash hits next year, a thirteen year recovery takes them to seventy-one. That's why the mix should change as the date gets closer.

That's not about being scared. It's about not being forced to sell at the bottom because you need the money for a house, a car, or your retirement.

The simplest tool for that isn't an ETF at all. It's an emergency fund. A few months of expenses in cash, so a broken car or a lost job never forces you to sell your ETF at minus forty percent.

Number two. Keep buying.

The monthly saver who kept going through 2002 and 2008 turned ninety-six thousand euros into about four hundred and sixteen thousand. The crashes were where most of that came from.

The practical way to do that is boring on purpose: a standing order on the same day every month, set up once, and then left alone. Most European brokers offer savings plans for free or close to it.

Number three. And this is the one that matters most. Not selling.

Let's meet two investors. Both put ten thousand euros into world stocks at the end of 1999.

At the end of 2002, with forty-five percent gone, investor A panics. Sells everything. Puts the five thousand five hundred euros left into a savings account paying two percent a year.

Investor B does nothing. Doesn't sell. Doesn't check the app. Just waits.

Today, investor A has about eight thousand eight hundred euros. Less than they started with, twenty-seven years later.

And investor B has forty-six thousand.

And here's the cruel part. Investor A didn't feel stupid in 2003. They felt smart. They had avoided the pain. Every bad headline for the next ten years told them they were right.

That's why panic selling is so dangerous. It feels like the responsible thing to do, and the bill only arrives many years later.
